newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House tax chair unveils tax cut legislation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House tax chair unveils tax cut legislation.

text.p: House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer proposed Monday an $85 billion tax cut package over five years that would affect capital gains, education, estate and income taxes.

The Texas Republican's bill was aimed at filling in the details of the tax portion of an agreement reached between congressional leaders and President Clinton to wipe out the budget deficit over five years.
The legislation will be the starting point for the committee which will work on the bill later this week in what could be the first tax cuts enacted since 1981.
"Tax relief and a balanced budget are on the way for the American people," Archer declared at a press conference.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said the Clinton administration had serious concerns with Archer's tax proposal and that he will work with Congress to overcome disagreements.
Republicans for years have wanted to cut the capital gains tax and see this as a key opportunity to accomplish that.

The maximum capital gains tax rate for individuals would be cut to 20 percent from the current 28 percent. The capital gains tax provision would take account of inflation for stocks and other assets bought by individuals starting Jan. 1, 2001.
"Indexing is the piece of capital gains that we are most troubled about," Rubin said, in part because of its potential long-term impact on government revenues.
For corporations, the capital gains tax rate would be reduced gradually from a maximum 35 percent to 30 percent in 2000 for assets held more than five years.
Archer kept the effective date for the capital gains tax cut of May 7.

"With the recent stock market boom, an increasing number of middle-class Americans are benefiting from the rising value of their stocks and mutual funds," Archer said. "Middle-income Americans need a capital gains tax cut, and I intend to give it to them."
Profits on selling homes of up to $500,000 for married couples would be excluded from the capital gains tax.

The capital gains provisions were expected to raise $2.7 billion for the government over the first five years on the expectation that investors would rush to sell assets initially and therefore pay tax on them.
The costs of the provisions increase over the following five years for a total cost of $35 billion over 10 years.

The most costly piece of the five-year tax package was a permanent tax credit for children under age 17 that would be $400 in fiscal 1998 and $500 after that. The cost over five years of that proposal would be $71 billion.
In trying to fulfil a promise by the Republican leadership to Clinton to include "roughly" $35 billion in higher education tax initiatives, Archer proposed $31 billion over five years.
Rubin said Archer's tax plan was not consistent with the agreement on education incentives made with congressional leaders.

Archer's package included about $47 billion in revenue increases over five years from airline ticket taxes, departure fees and reducing the ethanol tax credit. Also Archer proposed imposing a federal tax on income earned by Indian tribes from commercial activities including gaming.
Archer's tax plan would cut individual income taxes by a net $19.7 billion in 1998.
The ranking Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee criticised Archer's plan. Representative Charles Rangel, a New York Democrat, said: "He's just pushed this envelope so far to the right."
Rangel said he had thought two to three Democrats on the committee might vote with Archer, but after seeing the bill said he was not sure any of them would vote for it if the president opposed it.
The tax bill would phase in an increase of the threshold at which the estate tax kicks in to eventually reach $1 million from the current $600,000.
The Archer bill would also create an "American Dream" savings accounts which would allow tax-free withdrawals for first-time home purchases.
